text: Basic material (Type I only). The basic material for the Type I coat shall be a 50/50 nylon/cotton blend, wind resistant poplin ripstop cloth in a Universal Camouflage Pattern (UCP) conforming to Class 8, or Operation Enduring Freedom Camouflage Pattern (OEF-CP) conforming to Class 11, or Operational Camouflage Pattern (OCP) conforming to Class 14 of MIL-DTL-44436 as specified (see 6.2). Basic material (Type II only). The basic material for the Type II coat shall be a 65/25/10 Flame Resistant (FR) rayon/para-aramid/nylon blend ripstop cloth in a Universal Camouflage Pattern (UCP) conforming to GL-PD-07-12 Type I, Class 1, or Operation Enduring Freedom Camouflage Pattern (OEF-CP) conforming to Type I, Class 2, or Operational Camouflage Pattern (OCP) conforming to Type I, Class 3 as specified (see 6.2).
embed_text:

Basic material (Type I only). The basic material for the Type I coat shall be a 50/50 nylon/cotton blend, wind resistant poplin ripstop cloth in a Universal Camouflage Pattern (UCP) conforming to Class 8, or Operation Enduring Freedom Camouflage Pattern (OEF-CP) conforming to Class 11, or Operational Camouflage Pattern (OCP) conforming to Class 14 of MIL-DTL-44436 as specified (see 6.2). Basic material (Type II only). The basic material for the Type II coat shall be a 65/25/10 Flame Resistant (FR) rayon/para-aramid/nylon blend ripstop cloth in a Universal Camouflage Pattern (UCP) conforming to GL-PD-07-12 Type I, Class 1, or Operation Enduring Freedom Camouflage Pattern (OEF-CP) conforming to Type I, Class 2, or Operational Camouflage Pattern (OCP) conforming to Type I, Class 3 as specified (see 6.2).

text: Basic material (Type III only). The construction for coats shall be made in accordance to paragraphs 3.7.1 - 3.7.13. Construction is for all types, styles and classes unless otherwise noted. All garment material edges shall be clean finished, either, turned-in, turnedunder or serged unless otherwise indicated. All components with a grain line shall follow the grain line of the basic garment material or as indicated on pattern.

text: 3.7.1 Fastener tape (hook and loop). All widths of hook and loop tape shall be sewn 1/8-inch to 3/16-inch from bound selvage (for fastener tape with selvage) or from tape edge (for fastener tape without selvage) to prevent needle cutting along edges, stitching runoffs or improper fit into automatic sewing equipment. To prevent raveling on fastener tape with selvage, do not sew directly on the selvage. The use of fastener tape that is slit, has split edges, or any splicing of fastener tape is not permitted. Under no circumstances shall any fastener tape be re-stitched for repair purposes. New tape shall be used for repairs to prevent needle cutting, thus offering maximum field life. All fastener tape may be sewn through all layers on coat as indicated on the figures, (see patterns for placement). Tolerance for all lengths shall be (±1/8) inch.

text: 3.7.2 Collar. The collar (see figure 3) shall be interlined with a fusible as specified in 3.3.2. 3.7.3 Front closure. The front closure is a (double slider) slide fastener with a secondary hook and loop tape closure (see figure 1). The secondary closure consists of three (3) pairs of hook and loop fastener tape. The hook portion is on the underside of the front overlapping facing (left side) and is additionally stitched with a box-x stitch. The loop portion is stitched to the front side of the under facing (right side) and is additionally stitched with a box-x stitch and coincides with the hook. The hook and loop fasteners for the front closure shall be 1-inch wide by 1-1/2-inches in length. See pattern for placement. 3.7.3.1 Front facing. As an option the overlapping facing may be fused (see Tables IVA and IVB).

text: 3.7.4 Upper sleeve pockets. Both upper sleeve pockets shall have a slide fastener. 3.7.4.1 Upper sleeve pocket. The sleeve pocket shall have a bellows at front, back and bottom with a slide fastener opening and eyelet at the bottom right of bellow. The pocket shall finish 5 (± 3/16) inches in width and 7-1/4 (± 3/16) inches in length. Each pocket shall have a 4inch wide by 6-1/2-inch cut length loop fastener tape sewn on all sides, positioned 3/8-inch from bottom and top of pocket and centered side to side. The loop tape shall be additionally stitched with a crisscrossed-X pattern of stitching (see figure 4). See pattern for pocket loop fastener tape and eyelet placement.

text: 3.7.5 Sleeve cuff. The sleeve cuff shall be as specified in the pattern. The main body of the sleeve cuff shall have three (3) buttonholes spaced as per pattern. The sleeve cuff shall have a pointed adjustable tab with one (1) button sewn to the underside for closure adjustment (see figures 1 and 2). The sleeve tabs shall be 2-1/8 (± 1/8) inches wide by 3-1/8 (± 1/8) in length for all sizes. 3.7.5.1 Buttonholes. The buttonholes shall be eyelet-end tapered bar type (eyelet end toward the cuff edge-see figure 2) worked over gimp for the cuff with not less than four (4) tacking stitches at bar end catching the gimp ends (not counting the crossover stitch). The purling shall be on the inside surface. The cut lengths shall be 3/4 to 7/8-inch. The buttonholes shall be clean cut with the stitching securely caught in fabric.

The nylon tape shall be of sufficient length to cover the IFF material when the hook is engaged. See IFF webbing template (Table IVA and Table IVB) and pattern for placement. The IFF material shall be in accordance with 3.7.10.1. 3.7.10.1 Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) material. text: 3.11.1 Seams and stitching. All seams shall be consistent and exhibit a uniform appearance and conform to the ASTM D 6193 seam and stitch types listed in Table V. The backside of seams (inside garment) shall be flat with no protruding seam allowance to create irritation or discomfort. All material edges shall be clean finished, either, turned-in, turned-under or serged. All pocket flaps shall be serged prior to setting. Needle and bobbin thread tension shall be balanced such that neither is too tight nor too loose relative to each other. The seams for all outside visible stitching shall be sewn with 11 (± 1) stitches per inch. Overedge or pre-hemming shall be 10 (± 2) stitches per inch. Buttons shall be attached with 16 stitches per button. Buttonholes shall be 54 (± 2) stitches per inch including tack. All hook and loop tape shall be sewn with 10 (± 2) stitches per inch.

text: Repairs of stitching. Repairs of stitching shall be as follows: When thread breaks or bobbin run-outs occur during stitching, the stitching shall be repaired by restarting the stitching a minimum of 1/2-inch in back of the end of the stitching. Thread breaks or two (2) or more consecutive skipped or run-off stitches noted during end item inspection shall be repaired by overstitching. The stitching shall start at a minimum of 1/2-inch in back of the defective area and continue a minimum of 1/2-inch beyond the defective area onto the existing stitching. Loose or excessively tight stitching shall be repaired by removing the defective stitching, without damaging the materials, and restitching in the required manner.

text: Verify that the percent recovery of permethrin for any specimen size and composition, is 95% or greater by comparing the recovery level from the first extraction, to that of subsequent extractions. Combine the permethrin levels obtained from each of the three extractions, if the initial extraction yields permethrin levels 95% or greater than the total percent of permethrin extracted three sequential times, then the extraction efficiency is 95% or greater. Note - To ensure that the extraction efficiency is being accurately calculated, the permethrin levels in the second and third extraction should be minimal, and the permethrin level by the third extraction should be trace or zero.

Percent (%) bite protection shall be measured on a finished permethrin treated garment, Class 2, under three (3) test conditions and using a control specimen (non-permethrin treated, garment, Class 1) against the two (2) selected insect species specified in 4.5.2.3. text: 4.5.2.3.3.1 Insect characteristics. Mosquito ages employed for these studies shall be 5 to 11 days old after emergence from the pupal stage. Mosquitoes shall be laboratory-reared and disease free, and have been kept in stock cages containing both males and females. The mosquitoes will be maintained on 10% sugar water and have not been provided a blood meal. Methods should be used to preselect females for the studies. Use either a hand draw box or suitable aspirating device to collect host-seeking mosquitoes for the required cage density (see 4.5.2.3.3.3). 4.5.2.3.3.2 Insect rearing. Insects for these studies shall be reared under optimal conditions for larvae, as described in OPPTS 810.3700, section (d)(1)(iii).

text: 4.5.2.3.3.3 Cage conditions. A cage density of 200 (±25) female insects per cage is required to meet the biting pressure density of at least one (1) female mosquito per 300 cm 3 cage volume. (Cages shall be 60,000 (±6,000) cm 3 , with a sleeved opening for the arm of the volunteer to be inserted.) Cages shall be constructed of a lightweight clear plastic on three (3) sides, or an aluminum bottom panel with light weight clear plastic on two (2) sides. The top of the cage and side opposite the cloth sleeve should consist of screen rather than plastic. Tests shall be conducted with fluorescent lights on and under room conditions (22-27 o C, and 30-80% RH). Tests should not be conducted if the temperature or humidity is outside of the specified range.

The same three (3) subjects can be used to evaluate different insect species done at the same facility. Due to the replication, the number of volunteers is now decreased from the five (5) or more recommended in OPPTS 810.3700, section (c)(3)(i). Collection of data from both females and males are preferred for the study. Cosmetics and alcohol shall be avoided 12 hours prior and during the test. text: 4.5.2.3.5 Volunteer's test area. The test area shall consist of the region from the wrist to approximately 1/2-inch before the elbow. Fabric material shall be secured around the forearm to eliminate gaps between the arm and material and with the fastened seam positioned on the top of the forearm as specified in 4.5.2.3.2. The ends of the garment, near the wrist and elbow shall be sealed with protective tape of adequate thickness to prevent insects from biting through the tape. The hand shall be gloved with a glove of appropriate thickness to prevent biting through to the hand.

text: 4.5.2.3.6 Controls. For each set of specimen, a control shall be conducted. The control shall consist of the same fabric as the specimen, will not be laundered and will not contain the insect protection treatment. It will be identical in size to the test swatch (see 4.5.2.2). Controls will be cut in clean area and stored in separate plastic bags to avoid residual permethrin contamination. The controls will be tested on the arm opposite the treated specimen, or on the same arm used for experiments provided that the control is tested prior to testing treated specimens.

text: 4.5.2.3.7 Biting exposure. Arms containing the controls and treated specimen shall be exposed to a cage of insects for 15 minutes. The order of testing specimens on the arm will be sequential and in order of the most laundered to least laundered. Therefore, if the same arm will be used to test the control and specimens, the order of testing shall be control, followed by the specimen laundered 50 cycles, followed by the specimen laundered 20 cycles, and then conclude with testing the unlaundered treated specimen. Tests should be conducted with as little elapsed time as possible in between testing of a volunteer's arms.

text: Machine installation should only be carried out by a qualified technician. Contact your Brother dealer or a qualified electrician for any electrical work that may need to be done. The sewing machine weighs approximately 34.5 kg (76lb). The installation should be carried out by two or more people. Do not connect the power cord until installation is complete. The machine may operate if the treadle is depressed by mistake, which could result in injury. Turn off the power switch before inserting or removing the plug, otherwise damage to the control box could result. Be sure to connect the ground. If the ground connection is not secure, you run a high risk of receiving a serious electric shock, and problems with correct operation may also occur.

text: If using thick thread, or if the thread is not being trimmed, adjust the tilt of the upper knife (10) forward. Adjust the positions of the upper and lower knife holders so that the upper knife (10) and the lower knife (6) mesh and the tips of both knives are aligned at the center of the needle. text: Machine installation should only be carried out by a qualified technician. Contact your Brother dealer or a qualified electrician for any electrical work that may need to be done. The machine may operate if the treadle is depressed by mistake, which could result in injury. Turn off the power switch before inserting or removing the plug, otherwise damage to the control box could result. Be sure to connect the ground. Be sure to wear protective goggles and gloves when handling the lubricating oil and grease, so that they do not get into your eyes or onto your skin, otherwise inflammation can result. Furthermore, do not drink the oil or eat the grease under any circumstances, as they can cause vomiting and diarrhea. Keep the oil out of the reach of children. When cutting the nozzle of the oil tank, hold the base of the nozzle securely. If you hold the end of the nozzle, injury from the scissors may result. section: 5-5. Using program individual functions and program common functions
text: ・ In addition to start backtack sewing, main sewing and end backtack sewing, the following 8 types of functions are also included in the parameters which are necessary for sewing. Needle up/down, thread trimming lock, correction sewing, AUTO, slow start, special locus, bird's nest reduction mode, short trailing thread mode. ・ Of these 8 types of functions, the functions which can be set separately for each program are called "program individual" functions. When an assignment is made to a program individual function, a "P" symbol appears in the top-left corner of the icon. On the other hand, the functions which can be set in common for all programs (P1 to P9) are called "program common" functions. ・ Each of the 8 types of functions can be set to be used as either a program individual function or a program common function. (Memory switches MSW-301 to MSW-309)

text: Problem: 5 | Problem: Skipped stitches at sewing start Thread unraveling at sewing start. 0749M | Possible cause: ・ Is the thread take-up spring tension too strong? Reduce the tension of the thread take-up spring. ・ Is the thread take-up spring operating range too large? Lower the position of the thread take-up spring. ・ Is the trailing length of the upper thread too short after thread trimming? Adjust the pretension. ・ Are the threads not being trimmed cleanly? Sharpen the fixed knives, or replace the fixed and movable knives if necessary. Replace the movable knife. ・ Is the needle too thick? Replace the needle with a needle that is one rank thinner. ・ Is the length of thread trailing out from the bobbin case after thread trimming too short If the bobbin is spinning loosely, replace the anti-spin spring in the bobbin case. ・ Is the sewing speed too fast at the sewing start? Use the slow start key. ・ Is the needle up stop position too high? Adjust the needle up stop position. ・ Is the upper thread trailing length too short after thread trimming? Turn on the thread pull-out prevention function. ・ If the thread is pulling out at the sewing start, try the following remedies. 1. Check the upper thread trailing length. 2. Set the slow start number to "3" or less. 3. Re-adjust the upper thread trailing length to make it longer. 4. Keep pressing the bird's nest reduction mode key (3), and then select "Prev. thread away PARA" from "Best PFM mode setting". (1) Set the 2nd stitch pitch to "3". (2) Increase the current stitch pitch settings for the 1st and 2nd stitches by about 0.5 to 1. ・ Is the needle hole in the needle plate too large for the needle being used? Replace the needle place with one with a needle hole that is one rank thinner. ・ Is the presser foot groove too wide? Replace the presser foot with one that has a narrower groove so that it presses the material at the needle drop position. ・ Is the sewing machine starting to sew before the presser foot has dropped? The following instructions are planned in sequence in so far as is possible, to guide the home sewer in the construction of a suit, a coat, or slacks. Not all instructions in basic sewing can be included in this manual, since there are adequate texts already available. This manual, with its illustrations, should assist one in developing better constructions in tailoring, give one an appreciation of what goes into a custom-made garment, and aid one in the selection of future ready-made suits, coats, and slacks. Shrinking All wool fabrics, whether labeled preshrunk or not, should be shrunk before being made into a garment. Each end of fabric must be torn or cut along the thread before shrinking to save loss of yardage. This may be suggested to the clerk when purchasing fabric. Open up fabric and press along crease. After being pressed, the fabric will still be slightly damp; spread it smoothly on cutting table to dry thoroughly, having both cross and length grains parallel to table edges. Wet one half of a sheet and wring out; then fold the dry end into the wet end and wring again until the sheet is evenly damp all over. Canvas, linen tape, grosgrain belting: To shrink canvas, fold the material loosely back and forth like an accordion and submerge into container of hot water, allowing to stand until cold.

Each end of fabric must be torn or cut along the thread before shrinking to save loss of yardage. This may be suggested to the clerk when purchasing fabric. Open up fabric and press along crease. After being pressed, the fabric will still be slightly damp; spread it smoothly on cutting table to dry thoroughly, having both cross and length grains parallel to table edges. text: Smooth out the sheet on cutting table. Lay the folded wool along the edge of wet sheet and fold the remaining sheet width over the top of the wool. Remove from water bath, strip water out by hand, roll in cloth or spread smoothly on flat surface to dry partially before ironing. Loosely fold the sheet and wool together and allow to stand at least six hours, preferably overnight. Do not wring out the materials from water bath; this causes wrinkles which are difficult to iron out. Remove wool from sheet, and while damp pull it diagonally into shape until the folded edges and ends of wool lie square with the table. Keep the grain of material parallel with table edges while ironing. Loosely woven woolens will not need to be pressed and may be left to dry on table.

text: Because it is difficult for a person to fit herself, and a fitter is not always available, a dress form the exact duplicate of one’s figure is almost essential. One that is made on the individual is more satisfactory and less expensive than the commercially made form. For that reason, the instructions for making a form have been included in this tailoring manual. Method of procedure: Four persons are necessary to construct the form quickly; two to moisten strips, and two to paste strips to person, one working on the front and one on the back. Allow one hour for making the form on the figure and one hour for finishing it after it is removed from the figure. The person should wear a bra and girdle which give desirable style lines. She should stand so that her hands may be placed on the back of a chair or rest on the edge of a table for support. Figure 2. Materials needed:

text: Figure 4 (b) Measuring the Commercial Pattern Since commercial patterns vary in size, each pattern used should be carefully measured and checked against figure measurements to insure correct size and fit. This should be done before any alterations are attempted. All body measurements are taken in full circumference. Commercial patterns produce only half the figure pattern for the front and back jacket and for skirt; hence care must be taken when reducing the matching figure measurements. All seam lines should be carefully marked on the pattern so as not to include seams, when measuring the pattern, or all seams may be trimmed away from the pattern edge for measurements. Surplus tissue around the cutting edges of any pattern pieces should be cut away before trying to use the pattern. Each grain marking should be ruled the full length of pattern piece for accuracy in measuring.

text: To eliminate any hazards in construction, it is wise to construct a muslin jacket or upper part of a coat before cutting into the fabric itself. In a coat of princess lines, the entire garment should be made first in muslin. Although this method takes somewhat longer in the construction process, it is justified because it eliminates the possibility of mistakes likely to occur with even the most careful sewer. Refer to page 38 for suggested seam allowances, and mark seams out beyond muslin edge before cutting. Cut the entire muslin garment. All edge notches should be cut out of instead of into the seam edge. All length grains are marked along a ruled line on the muslin since the muslin will be used in place of the tissue when cutting the wool garment.

text: Heavy unbleached muslin or similar material is used for this purpose. The muslin is cut from the altered pattern, marked, and basted (using long machine stitch or hand basting). The muslin garment is fitted as accurately as the garment itself. The collar and both sleeves are fitted into the garment. CUTTING THE MUSLIN JACKET For cutting one should use shears about 8 inches long, with sharp edges and a fine point for clipping. Cutting should be done with fabric lying flat on the table and with the full length of the blade. The muslin should be torn across each end, pulled into shape, and pressed before any cutting is done. It should be folded right side in, so that all markings, except center front and back, appear on wrong side.

text: For fitting, all bastings should be done with short even stitches, using heavy-duty thread that is stronger and smoother than regular white basting cotton. A contrasting color is advisable, for it is more easily seen than a matching color. On white or pastels, a pastel-colored thread should be used as some dark colors may crock and stain the fabric when steamed. If tailor tacks are made of contrasting darning cotton, take only one stitch as it does not slide from the fabric. If made of a basting thread, take two tiny stitches through the two thicknesses, leaving a loop and thread ends about lh inch long on the wrong side of the garment. text: If bust, chest, or other parts of the figure need wadding to smooth out the figure, these sections should be cared for in this first fitting. In the raglan, kimono, or dolman, the sleeves are basted into position for the first fitting. See padding problems in Fig. 20, p. 42. text: To fit a skirt, first measure the belt around the waist and baste across the two matching ends; also mark second side seam, center front, and back with bastings. Pin the skirt to the belt before trying on for first fitting. Try on and fit skirt down to widest hips. Remove, baste fitted section, then rule remaining seams up from skirt bottom and continue basting with the grain. Try on for readjustments. FITTING THE JACKET OR COAT A suit jacket should be fitted over a blouse or sweater; and a coat should be fitted over a dress or over a suit, if suits are to be worn under the coat. To hang the skirt, adjust to the figure, use table edge as a guide, and mark with pins around the skirt at table top. Measure from table edge to floor, subtract the distance from floor that the skirt is to be worn, and measure skirt hem edge parallel to pins at hip.

text: General Suggestions in Garment Construction Some persons will need to fill out hollows in the figure with padding to create more pleasing results in the outward appearance of the garment. This should be done in the first fitting. Tailoring requires the best of one’s sewing ability, in accuracy of details, in correct fitting, straight stitching and careful steaming of each step in garment construction. Inaccurate work¬ manship stands out much more readily in a tailored garment than in a soft wool dress. Uneven or unmatched lapels, poorly pad stitched lapels or collar, poorly made pockets or buttonholes are all noticeable in a tailored garment. A garment will look just as good as the construction processes put into it, and there are no short cuts if one wishes to have a beautiful garment.

text: Use either a steam iron without press cloth or a plain iron with a press cloth. With each, use a moderately warm iron, never a hot one. An iron too hot will scorch wool through a press cloth even though the press cloth will show no scorch. Where a seam appears at an edge turn, baste the seam along fold turn, slightly rolling seam to the wrong side to prevent stitching edge from showing from the right side. Steam the seam from the wrong side. After the seam is steamed, remove bastings and resteam to remove basting imprints. This is essential as the imprints are difficult to remove if allowed to dry. When imprints are stubborn to remove, they may be steamed along the edge, pounded with a wooden paddle or by hand, then resteamed. Use the paddle also to flatten out bulky spots, such as buttonholes or sharp turns in a seam.

text: When a tailored garment is ready for the lining, a final all-over steaming may be necessary. It is difficult to give some fabrics a sharp steamed edge; therefore, it is advisable to take the finished garment for a final steaming to your favorite dry cleaner who has commercial equipment. The presser should be warned, however, that this is a newly made garment and that special care should be taken in its steaming. Making the Skirt BASTING THE SKIRT If the skirt has pleats, baste and steam the pleats before basting seams. Pin the marked pleat edge from waist to skirt bottom and baste along folded edge. Steam the basted fold along a ruled line, remove basting, and resteam to remove basting imprints. Match folded pleat edge into position, pin and baste fold to skirt the entire skirt length.

text: There are several methods of finishing a skirt at the waistline, depending upon the desires of the wearer and upon fashions. Whichever method is chosen, the skirt must be fitted onto the belt or its equivalent. Any one of the following methods may be chosen: The belt must have two hooks and eyes to fasten the underlap, and may have hooks and eyes or button and buttonhole for the overlap. a. Belt can be made entirely of the fabric. This belt is cut 3 or 4 inches longer than waist measure and twice as wide as the finished belt width, plus the width of seams at ends and sides. c. Shaped facing in a skirt where skirt top extends above waistline. This type of waistline finish varies with fashion and must have a stiff inner fitted facing of buckram, horsehair, or the equivalent.

text: If the skirt and belt have been tailor-tacked and separated in order to stitch the seams and make the placket, rebaste the two together by matching corresponding tailor tacks. Stitch the skirt to the under belt from the wrong side along the lower belt edge. If the skirt belt of the fabric is to have a piped or corded buttonhole, make this buttonhole before stitching the outer belt facing into place. Face the end of the belt receiving the buttonhole with a piece of canvas long enough to receive the buttonhole. (See directions for buttonholes on pp. 78-80.) A corded buttonhole is difficult to make where grosgrain is used but a worked buttonhole is satisfactory. After the buttonhole is on the right side of the belt end, baste the top belt into place and stitch along the belt edge either by machine or slip stitch by hand.

text: Place a damp cloth over hem, or use a steam iron, and shrink away surplus fullness of hem. Push the iron from fold upward to cut edge to shrink out as much as possible of the surplus ease. MARKING THE HEM OF THE SKIRT Adjust skirt to figure and fasten all openings as they are to be worn when finished. HEM FINISHES To secure a more even hemline, have the model stand erect with weight balanced evenly on both feet. Using skirt marker, rule, or square, mark the garment hem parallel to the floor, placing pins 2 or 3 inches apart. The person marking the hemline should move around the model, for the model may shift position when turning and cause an uneven hemline. Figure 35. The hem may be finished in any one of various ways, according to the texture of the fabric. Stitches in wool hems should be lA inch apart, with very tiny stitches taken in the wool, and the thread left easy along the hemming edge.

text: Sometimes in commercial patterns the spaces between buttonholes are not accurate, or one may wish to shift the buttonholes either up or down, or change the number indicated on the pattern. To be sure of accuracy, mark the top and bottom positions of buttonholes on the garment and then accurately divide and mark between these two marks for the desired number of buttonholes. If the buttonholes end at the waist or continue below, place a buttonhole at the low waistline to add apparent length to the figure. In women’s garments the right side carries the buttonholes and overlaps onto the left, which holds the buttons. The end of the buttonhole should extend slighdy over the center front line toward the garment edge. This extension should be one half the width of the shank of the button when sewn to the garment, which is approximately Vi 6 of an inch. Figure 40.

In a corded or piped pocket use bias because it adjusts more easily to that type of pocket. The bias should always be cut in the same direction from the fabric. With the garment on the wearer, turn the hem up before the permanent location of the pockets is decided upon. Mark the new pocket location accurately on one side of the garment. Always cut the grain of the pocket bag the same as the garment grain. In an inset pocket, one section of the bag is usually of wool and one of lining. Because all persons are not the same size, these positions may need to be changed to keep them in correct proportion to the wearer. In a corded or piped pocket use bias because it adjusts more easily to that type of pocket. The bias should always be cut in the same direction from the fabric. With the garment on the wearer, turn the hem up before the permanent location of the pockets is decided upon. Mark the new pocket location accurately on one side of the garment. Always cut the grain of the pocket bag the same as the garment grain. In an inset pocket, one section of the bag is usually of wool and one of lining. To save wool, a narrow strip of wool may be stitched across the upper pocket lining bag instead of making the section entirely of wool.

text: Remove the garment and pin together, accurately matching the two front sections of the garment; and transfer the marked pocket position to the second half of the garment. If one hip is larger, the garment may be wider on one side of the pocket position. This variance in width should appear from the pocket edge to the side seam of the garment. When a pocket is parallel to the floor, the wool section is always sewed to the upper edge, the lining to the lower edge of a pocket.

text: All set-in pockets should be reinforced with canvas along the stitching line on the wrong side of the garment. This canvas prevents too great strain on the fabric. The pocket above the bust line already has canvas behind it, but pockets below the waistline will need to be reinforced. In a patch pocket, reinforce the two top comers with canvas on the wrong side of the fabric. Cut the canvas on the same grain as the fabric it is reinforcing. In a perpendicular pocket the wool section is sewed to the back edge, the lining to the front edge of the pocket opening. Check pocket size and length in relationship to the size and scale of the individual. WELT POCKET Figure 59. A welt pocket is made with the welt sewed into the lower edge of an inserted pocket, which may be parallel to the floor, perpendicular to the floor, or on the diagonal.

text: Bias must all be cut in one direction; otherwise, when joining the bias in a seam or in making buttonholes or pockets, the design in the twill, stripe, or plaid will not match. It is recommended that a trial sample be made on a scrap of material to see which gives the best effect before applying to the garment. When facing the inside of a garment, ease the garment slightly onto the facing. When using the facing on the outside of the garment, ease slightly onto the garment. Bias is cut twice the width of the finished edge plus two seams. Stitch all seams in the facing and steam open before applying to the garment, and match all seams. Place the bias to the garment edge with right sides facing and stitching edges matching. Stretch the bias slightly onto the garment edge to prevent fullness on the bias edge. Pin and baste into position and miter any angle turns.

text: FASTENING SHOULDER PADS TO GARMENT After the sleeves are stitched at armscye, put the garment on dress form or figure and permanently adjust both shoulder pads into position under the front facing. Usually the outer edge of pad extends approximately xh inch beyond armscye stitching edge, depending on fashion and appearance. Pin securely into position from right side of garment so that when the pad is sewed to garment there will be no slippage. On an outside curved edge ease the bias slightly along the stitching edge to allow folded edge of the bias to lie flat when finished. On an inside curve stretch the bias slightly to prevent the fold edge of the bias from rippling. Machine stitch from garment side along marked stitching edge. Steam the bias away from the stitching line toward the cut edge.

Usually the outer edge of pad extends approximately xh inch beyond armscye stitching edge, depending on fashion and appearance. Pin securely into position from right side of garment so that when the pad is sewed to garment there will be no slippage. On an outside curved edge ease the bias slightly along the stitching edge to allow folded edge of the bias to lie flat when finished. On an inside curve stretch the bias slightly to prevent the fold edge of the bias from rippling. Machine stitch from garment side along marked stitching edge. Steam the bias away from the stitching line toward the cut edge.

text: Pads are sewed to canvas from armscye toward neck where point of pad is securely anchored to shoulder seam. Where the pad falls along armscye seam, sew the two together with a loose stab stitch and securely anchor each pad end to armscye seam, using a double strand of mercerized cotton. Measure from the stitching on the bias the exact width desired; fold the bias to the wrong side and baste along folded edge. From the wrong side of the garment, fold under the bias edge, leaving the bias just wide enough to cover the machine stitching, and baste into place. In a raglan or kimono sleeve use the curved shoulder pad and adjust it until it gives the best shoulder shape from right side of garment. Sew the pad securely to the shoulder seam or seams. text: A tailor or dry cleaner has adequate equipment which is not available to everyone. It is recommended that the finished garment be taken for a final steaming to be done by a tailor or dry cleaner. However, the operator should be warned that it is a newly made garment and that great pains should be taken when steaming. These operators have been found to be most co-operative and the appearance achieved is well worth the added cost. In fact this final steaming improves some garments to such an extent that it covers up poor workmanship. A professional steaming will help the appearance of a garment, and few laboratories or homes have equipment for this steaming.

text: Modern machinery is characterized not only by high productivity and efficiency, but also by high complexity. A more economical operation necessitates a good organization of technical maintenance and repairs of the available machines and equipment, and their proper adjustment according to prescribed technological procedures. Referring particularly to textile machinery, it should be said that it works under extremely difficult conditions, i.e. high speeds (the rotational speed of the shaft at open-end spinning is 60 000 m i n -1 and higher), high dynamic loads (such as obtained in scutchers, cards, drawing frames, and looms), etc. The majority of textile machines operate in a dust-laden atmosphere at high humidity. The working organs of textile machines are in direct contact with the processed raw materials which causes machine wear.

text: The proper lubrication of all rubbing machine parts is always important in order to ensure their faultless running especially under conditions where textile enterprises are working in more than two shifts which results in high loading on the machines. This causes the accelerated physical wear of working elements, mechanisms and parts of textile machines, and various disarrangements that result in the reduction of labour productivity, machine efficiency, and products quality. text: Defects of products reveal the kind of disarrangements in assemblies and mechanisms. So, for instance, ifthe yarn produced in a spinning frame is twitty, this means that there are disarrangements in Disarrangements in Machines 11 the drafting system, such as loose keys in the gears of the drive to the cylinders, broken teeth on the gears of the drive to the drafting system, and the eccentricity of pressure rollers. When in good condition and not subjected to the effect of ambient heat, machine assemblies usually heat up to 40-50°C. Heating-up to higher temperatures occurs due to improper mating of parts, their misalignment, small clearances, high specific loads and poor lubrication. The general technical condition of the equipment may be assessed indirectly by checking the duration of run-out, or the time of machine self-braking.

During the initial period I of machtine operaion, when new parts are run-in, there is a stronger wear; further, comes the period II when the speed of wearing is at its minimum, i.e. when the process stabilizes; and finally follows the period III, when wear is progressively increasing up to an emergency state so that the part may be brought completely out of use. text: High-frequency current (induction) hardening reduces for instance the wear of parts from ordinary gray iron by factor of 2 to 7. Nitriding, i.e. saturation of surface with nitrogen, imparts a high hardness to cast iron parts (a Brinell hardness of 700 to 800), a good wear resistance (the wear resistance increases by factor of 2- 2.6) and the resistance to corrosion caused by the moisture of the ambient atmosphere. The thermal chromizing, i.e. the saturation of the part surface with chromium at the account of the diffusion process (similarly to the saturation with carbon or cementation) increases the surface hardness of cast iron parts almost by factor of 14 and their wear resistance by factor of 6 to 8; moreover, the corrosion resistance is markedly improved.

text: Tempering is a heat treatment of steel which follows hardening, carburizing and cyaniding (case hardening), removes stresses, increases ductility and impact resistance, and decreases the tensile and yield strengths of the hardened material. Moreover it is treated by cold. The main kinds of chemical and heat treatment of steel and cast iron are carburizing, cyaniding, nitriding, aluminizing and chromizing. The chemical and heat treatment of metals and alloys is effected by their heating and keeping at high temperature in active solid, liquid, and gas mediums. Parts and tools are chemical and heat treated to increase their surface hardness and resistance with the tenacity (ductility) of interior layers preserved unchanged. Some kinds of chemical and heat treatment should be followed by other types of heat treatment (for instance, carburizing is followed by hardening and tempering, etc.).

Nonferrous antifriction alloys. Most of these alloys have approximately the same structure — a plastic mass with embedded hard particles. During operation the soft mass wears more rapidly than the hard particles and as a result a microrelief is formed with protru­ ding hard particles which carry the mating part, such as shaft in bearing. The oil circulates easier along the formed canals and cools quicker the rubbing surfaces carrying-away with it the products of wear. To nonferrous antifriction alloys relate: babbitts, antifriction bronze, brass, zink and aluminium alloys.

text: The babbitts are subdivided into the tin-base, lead-base and cadmium-base babbitts. They are used for lining in bearings. Bronze and brass are copper-base alloys. Bronzes are subdivided into casting and wrought bronzes as well as tin and tinless bronzes. Tin bronze is used for bearings (linings, bushings) operating under loads not over 5-8 MPa, average speeds (up to 3-4 m/s) and normal temperatures. Tin bronze may take impact loads (up to 15-25 MPa) and high speeds (up to 8 m/s). The aluminium-iron bronze is used at high temperatures (up to 200-250°C) and under high loads. Aluminium ferrous-manganese brass and silica-lead brass are used for parts operating under high specific loads (up to 10-30 MPa) and at slow speeds (3-4 m/s). Parts wearing against brass (shaft necks and worms) should have a hardened surface (by nitriding, cementation, and hardening).

text: The use of porous bearings in textile machines is highly expedient, considering that they are capable of operating a long time without additional lubrication. Not long ago a new material— a metal-base laminate— has found application; it is obtained by sintering a bronze spherical powder loosely strewn on a steel ribbon with copper plated surface. The life of parts made ofsuch a metal-base laminate by swaging is twice longer than that of parts made of usual metal ceramics. Parts of compressed wood easily absorb oscillation and are capable to withstand high impact loads. Moreover, the part (shaft) operating in couple with the part made of compressed wood (bearer) wears less than in rubbing against any other material. Parts of compressed wood are easily worked in. Waviness has the following effect on the wear: with an increse in the wave height the wear increases, but at the same time the scoring resistance of the rubbing surfaces is improved. The initial condition of the part (surface quality) changes in the course of operation (or wear). During machine parts working-in, the initial surface irregularities formed at machining are completely or partially eliminated, worn out and crushed; new irregularities appear with different shape, dimensions, and direction. If the con­ ditions of wear remain the same after working-in of the part, new irregularities differing from the initial ones appear on its surface.

text: Qualify of Machine Assembly, Operating Conditions, Lubrication and Maintenance Quality of machine assembly. Mistakes made during machine assembly affect the wear resistance of parts. Canting shafts, overtight bearings, misaligned multiple-seated shafts, improperly meshed gears, incorrectly matched cams, poor balancing of rotating parts may become a cause of the rapid wear of machine parts. A canting shaft at the beginning adheres only to the edges of the bearing so that a high specific load created at this point causes an intense heating and wear of parts. It should be taken into account that in case of shaft canting the liquid friction is impossible. If the shaft is of low rigidity, i.e. it m a y be easily bent, it is liable to be canted in the supports during operation even if the assembly has been done correctly. In this case self-adjustable bearings are used.

text: Lubrication of machines and their maintenance. As mentioned above, lubrication is intended for reducing the wear of machine parts. The effect obtained by lubrication in increasing the wear resistance of parts is considerable. For instance, lubrication brings about more than a 5-fold decrease in the wear of cast iron linings which were not worked-in, and of worked-in linings— more than 30 times. The lubricants are chosen taking into account the speed and design parameters of the parts. Thus, for instance when the choice is made for a couple shaft— hearing,the following factors shall be considered: the load, rotational speed of the shaft, clearance, thickness of lubricant layer, shaft diameter, and ratio of the bearing length and diameter.

text: The most important properties of lubricating oils is their viscosity. The greater are the load applied on the rubbing couple, the clearance, and the thickness of the lubricating layer, the higher must be the oil viscosity; the greater are the shaft rotational speed and diameter, and the ratio of the hearing length and diameter, the lower should be the oil viscosity. It must be taken into account that viscosity is not a stable characteristic which depends in a large measure on the temperature of the liquid lubricant and on the pressure. With an increase in the temperature, the viscosity is sharply reduced, especially in the temperature range from 0 to 40-60°C. Further, this drop in viscosity slows down, and at the temperatures above 80-100°C viscosity changes but little.

The wear of such parts as cast iron bearings and shafts due to the use of this oil is reduced from 3 to 4 times as compared with the wear of the same parts when ordinary mineral oil is used for the purpose. Moreover, the consumption of graphitized oil is twice smaller. It should be also noted that parts lubricated with graphitized oil are not subject to corrosion. The fatigue strength of parts is determined by the character and the intensity of variable load, the shape and dimensions of the part, the character of mating parts and the quality of their surface, the extent of corrosion, and the mechanical properties of the material from which the parts are made, their amenability to notching, and the technological process of part manufacturing. Character and intensity of variable load. The variable load acting on the part causes alternating stresses. Any single change in the stresses is called a cycle. The time during which the cycle is effected is called a period, and the number of cycles performed per unit of time (e.g., one minute) is called the cycle frequency.

text: The maximum stress at which the material is not destructed at the unlimited number of cycles is called the endurance limit, or the fatigue limit. At testing, this stress is set to 10-20 min cycles for steel, and 50-100 min cycles for nonferrous metals. If the part withstands the indicated number of cycles without cracking, it means that it is capable of withstanding an infinitely great number of cycles.

text: Overloading of parts affects in different ways the fatigue strength. With light overloads an increase in strength is observed, while with great overloads the strength is reduced. Ifthe stress is close to the endurance limit of parts which are not subjected to a constantly growing variable load, the fatigue resistance may considerably rise. This phenomenon is called the training of material. Consequently, working-in and running-in of assembled machines are necessary not only for working-in the rubbing surfaces of parts, but also for their training under the conditions of variable loads. In case of considerable overloads, i.e. stresses greatly exceeding the fatigue limit, the ability of metal to work without cracking under the action of cyclic loads, that is its endurance, noticeably decreases. text: Conjugation of parts. Close fits affect the fatigue strength more than all other factors: the fatigue strength may be decreased four times and more (the greater the interference, the less is the fatigue strength). At the same time the fatigue strength greatly depends on the kind of material from which the mating parts are made and on the kind of their conjugation. So for instance, the fatigue strength of the shaft decreases with the increase of the bush hardness; a longer or thinner hub, annular grooves on the butt of a pressed-on part, including the fit of parts on a special shoulder (thickening of the shaft) and the surface knurling of the shaft to fit parts are the factors which cause a decrease in the strength concentration.

text: Quality of part surface* The higher is the surface finish of the part, i.e. the less is its roughness, the greater is the fatigue resistance of the part. Stresses are concentrated on the rough surface of parts (in the cavity of every notch) which causes a decrease of its fatigue strength. Even inconsiderable scratches on a polished surface may cause a decrease in the endurance limit to 40%. Therefore, in repairs, the parts are subjected to artificial work-hardening owing to which their fatigue strength is increased from 1.5 to 2.5 times.

text: Corrosion. The surface corrosion of parts causes a considerable decrease in their endurance limit. The destruction of parts by corrosion is called corrosion fatigue. It increases when there is a concentration of stresses and the parts work in a more corroding medium, when the parts work in tension and compression, when the surface is coarse and the number of applied cycles is increased.

text: During the process of cutting not only irregularities are formed on> the surface, but also there occurs work-hardening of surface layers. Rolling effected by means of steel hardened rollers increases the fatigue resistance. The effect of forging on the steel strength depends on the direction of load application: the change in the amount of reduction by forging slightly affects the static strength and the impact strength of steel with the grain, while when the forging reduction ratio increases the impact strength of steel across the grain is considerably reduced. Consequently, the fatigue limit is less across thegrain than with the grain. Concentrated stresses have also a stronger effect on the longitudinal grain than upon the traverse ones.

text: Welded and built-up parts present a smaller endurance limit than whole parts made of the same metal. The endurance limit depends; on the method of welding. Electric arc welding ensures a higher endurance limit than gas welding (especially when heavy-coated electrodes are used); automatic welding permits us to obtain jointswith better endurance than manually welded joints; forging, annealing, machining and rolling of built-up metal also increase its endurance limit. The highest endurance limit is obtained at contact, flash welding.

text: Parts which in course of operation have lost their essential properties (dimensions and shape), with breakages etc., may be used for further operation after repairing. Any parts with different defects and disarrangements may be repaired. However, not all defectuous parts are repaired. The need of repair and the choice of the methods applied at the repairs are determined by economic considerations which are the cost of repairs and the longevity factor of the part. Modern technological processes used to restore parts not only allow the restitution of the parts, but also permit imparting them pro­ perties better than in the original parts.

text: Hot ringing ensures a better strength of the joint, as compared with the other methods. Moreover, the strength of joint between the ring and the part is influenced by the surface finish. For increasing the fatigue strength of parts restored by exterior ringing, the surface of the parts on which the ring is to be placed should be work-hardened or subjected to short-time nitriding. In case of excessive stresses, the negative allowance is reduced, the ring is welded around and work-hardened by means of a roller. When restoring the crankshaft rod nuts and split antifriction bearings, half-rings (half-bushings) are used. They are attached by welding, screws, and by other methods. In the case of exterior ringing, steel and cast-iron rings are employed, while for interior ringing bronze rings find application.

text: Stitchesorstrapsare used to stay the broken part. O n the both sides of the crack T, holes are drilled in which dowels 1(Fig. 5a) of the heated strap 2 (stitches or straps) are introduced; after cooling the strap tightens the crack. The number of straps used depends on the length of the crack. The distance between the holes must be smaller than the distance between the dowels (in a cold state), by the amount of interference fit. text: Knurling (Fig. 6e-f)is the process of plastic displacement of metal by pressing a steel roller into the corrugations of the part to be restored. W h e n restoring fluted rollers, a steel roller is forced into cavities between the flutes, and its rolling along the recess of the wornout flute displaces metal from hollows to the crest. Rolling. One or several easily rotating rollers with a smooth surface of hardened steel or hard alloy are pressed to the rotating cylindrical part lubricated with oil. The rollers are imparted not only with a rotational, but also with a translatory motion (along the surface of the part). The metal on the surface of the part is redistributed, and work-hardening of the surface layer takes place.

text: Straightenitig (Fig. 6g, h) is the restoration of a part which became bent or twisted in the course of operation. Straightening may be carried-out on cold and hot parts (the latter method is used in case of strong bending of the part). The accuracy of cold straightening is higher. Since the required sizes are not always obtained after cold straightening, it isrecommended to carry out stabilizing, i.e. heating of the parts after straightening to 400-500°C. Steel parts which are slightly bent are also straightened using surface cold-working. This kind of straightening is used for the repair of shafts, axles, knives, beams, guides, cylinders, and other parts.

text: There are two kinds of welding: fusion welding and pressure welding (plastic). To fusion welding pertain arc welding and gas welding- Pressure welding may be classified into resistance welding (butt, welding, seam welding and spot welding), gas pressure welding, and forge welding. The electric arc welding and gas welding are used for the repair (joining) of broken and cracked parts of steel, cast iron, bronze and other metals and alloys; the electric butt welding is used for butt joining of broken parts of steel and other plastic materials;: electric spot welding and seam welding are used for overlap joining of sheet materials.

To prepare parts for welding and surfacing, the joints are imparted the required shape for ensuring a sufficient cohesion between the original metal and the overlay. The method and kind of preparation depend on the character of the wear, the material, shape and size of parts. The edges of broken parts should be thoroughly prepared for different types of weld joints. The type of joint depends on the thickness of the part wall. W h e n the wall thickness <pis 1.5 m m or less the edges are not bevelled, when (pis 12 m m or less V joints are used, and when <pis more than 12 m m — double V joints are used. The fracture line is followed if one has to preserve the initial dimensions of the broken pieces.

text: Gas shielded-metal-arc welding is carried out as follows. Shielding gas (carbon dioxide, argon, hydrogen, and others) is constantly fed into the zone of the electric arc burning between the work and the electrode. The shielding gas displaces the air around the arc to protect molten metal against contamination with oxygen and nitrogen. Argon is used for building-up parts of high-alloy chrome-nickel steels, copper-, aluminium- and titanium-base alloys. The highest stability of the electric arc is obtained in that shielding gas. In carbon dioxide the arc stability is somewhat lower, and in hydrogen, it is minimum. The choice of the electrode wire depends on the kind of shielding gas. The gas shielded-metal-arc welder (carbon dioxide) consists of a bulb 1 (Fig. 10), heater 2t drier 3> step-down reducer 4, rotameter-flowmeter 5, and burner 6.

Argon is used for building-up parts of high-alloy chrome-nickel steels, copper-, aluminium- and titanium-base alloys. The highest stability of the electric arc is obtained in that shielding gas. In carbon dioxide the arc stability is somewhat lower, and in hydrogen, it is minimum. The choice of the electrode wire depends on the kind of shielding gas. The gas shielded-metal-arc welder (carbon dioxide) consists of a bulb 1 (Fig. 10), heater 2t drier 3> step-down reducer 4, rotameter-flowmeter 5, and burner 6.

text: Gas welding and building-up are used for restoring parts made of thin sheet steel 0.2-5 m m thick, low-melting (non-ferrous) metals and their alloys, of metals requiring gradual heating and slow cooling at welding (tool steels), and also metals requiring preheating before welding (cast iron and some grades of special steels). Moreover, this kind of repairs is used for hard facing with hard alloys and for brazing. A m o n g combustible gases the most frequently used is acetylene which when burning in mixture with oxygen develops a temperature of 3000 to 3200°C. At gas welding the molten metal absorbs oxygen and nitrogen from air less intensively than at electric arc welding. This is explained by the protective action ofthe flame and fluxes: the flame surrounding the metal melt attracts almost all the atmospheric oxygen necessary for the combustion of carbon and hydrogen.

text: Acetylene used for welding is obtained in acetylene generators directly at the point ofwelding, or brought in acetylene bottles. Usual­ ly for welding at repairs, a high-pressure portable generator is employed allowing the use of long hoses and welding burners of higher pressure and operation at low temperatures. Generators of all types have a water seal and a chemical cleaner. The water seal protects the generator from explosion because of backflash. The chemical cleaner is intended for purifying acetylene from hydrogen sulphide and hydrogen phosphate which are noxious impurities that would impair welding quality. Oxygen is supplied to the point of welding in special seamless steel bottles provided with pressure reducers. The main types of oxyacetylene torches are in common use today: the medium-pressure type and the low-pressure or injector type. 36 Chapter Two

text: Plasma hardfacing iscarried out by means of plasma torches having two arcs burning simultaneously, i.e. the plasma-forming arc and the arc for melting the work metal and the overlay metal. Surfacing is applied on parts made of low-carbon or chrome-nickel steel, aluminium alloy, etc. In electroslag building-up the current from the wire electrode passes to the work metal through the electroconducting liquid slag. The work to be surfaced is disposed vertically in parallel with a copper mould so that the clearance between the work surface and the mould is equal to the thickness of the built-up layer (not less than 10 mm). In this gap, a bath of liquid slag is formed in which heat is emitted. By displacing the mould gradually in vertical direction the entire gap is filled with the metal. This method is used for restoring badly worn out parts of cylindrical, conical and flat shape.

text: The kind of welding (arc, gas, etc.), the types of weld joints, their shape and dimensions must correspond to the technical requirements and standards. The area where metal is to be cut must be clean of all foreign matter such as moisture, rust, dirt, oil grease, and paint primer. Works made of sheet, bar, and structural rolled shapes must be checked, and ifnecessary straightened. Hot bending of rolled shapes (angles, rods and sheets) must be completed at a temperature not under 800°C. After heating, the work must be slowly and uniformly cooled to avoid hardening, warping, or cracking. Prior to welding, the joint edges must carefully be cleaned from dirt, rust, scale, and oil using steel brushes or other means.

text: In automatic submerged welding (under a layer of flux), it is necessary to clean with special care the edges to be welded as well as the adjoining metal over a width of 10-15 m m from both sides. After gas cutting, the edges of parts to be welded must be cleaned from bends of metal and adhering slag to the clean metal, and the burrs and irregularities on the joined surfaces must be eliminated. The adherence of parts must be regular over the entire length of the weld. In manual single-side butt-welding the fill on the other side of the weld must have the shape of a uniform roll throughout the whole seam length. In double-side butt welding, after the seam has been obtained, the fill on the other side of the joint must be cut away and cleaned with a steel brush. When welding with a multilayer seam, the surface of each layer must be cleaned from slag before applying the following one.

text: In inspecting welded structures, loaded seams must be examined with a magnifying glass over the whole weld length; and the seams which do not carry loads must be inspected over not less than 1/3 of their length. Simultaneously, the dimensions of the seam and its quality are checked by knocking with a hammer weighing 0.5-0.8 kg Methods of Machine Parts Restoration 37 and with a handle 300 m m long. The sound emitted on knocking the weld metal with a hammer must be the same, as when knocking the intact metal. When defective parts are detected— poor fusion of fill metal, cracks of any shape and delamination, porosity or slag inclusions— they are cut away and welded anew. Portions with strongly irregular seams, faults, waviness and sharply defined boundaries of scales must also be cut out and welded anew.

text: The process of metal coating consists of two operations: preparing the surface and spraying it with metal. The preparation of surface is carried out as follows. The part is cleaned from dirt (washed in kerosene or other solvents). Cast iron parts operating with ample lubrication are heated in a hearth or with a gas burner to a temperature of 200 to 250°C for extracting the oil from the pores. W h e n preparing parts which are bodies of revolution the irregularities of the worn-out surface (ovality, conicity, burrs, etc.) are eliminated by cutting on lathe machines. Next the surface is made rough, by cutting on it a “drunken thread”,or annular grooves. Roughing of parts with hard surfaces (hardened or cement-hardened) is achieved by means of the electric sparkor short-circuiting (vibration) methods. Parts of more complicated or flat shape are shot- or sandblasted.

The process of metal coating consists of two operations: preparing the surface and spraying it with metal. The preparation of surface is carried out as follows. The part is cleaned from dirt (washed in kerosene or other solvents). Cast iron parts operating with ample lubrication are heated in a hearth or with a gas burner to a temperature of 200 to 250°C for extracting the oil from the pores. W h e n preparing parts which are bodies of revolution the irregularities of the worn-out surface (ovality, conicity, burrs, etc.) are eliminated by cutting on lathe machines. Next the surface is made rough, by cutting on it a “drunken thread”,or annular grooves. Roughing of parts with hard surfaces (hardened or cement-hardened) is achieved by means of the electric sparkor short-circuiting (vibration) methods. Parts of more complicated or flat shape are shot- or sandblasted.

text: The essence ofthis method comes to the following. When two metal electrodes connected to different poles of the power source (anode and cathode) are brought together, a high voltage electric field is created causing a strong electric discharge. As a result, the metal in the shape of a liquid drop is ejected from the electrode acting as an anode and is transferred to the electrode acting as a cathode. If the anode (tool) is a rod of hard alloy or of any other current conducting material, its particles which are detached on the formation of the electric spark discharge are brought on the cathode (i.e. the part to be restored) and stay fast on the surface of the work. As a result, a new layer is formed on the surface of the workpiece, the properties of this layer being dependent on the properties of the anode material.

text: Electroplating. From all the available kinds of electroplating, chromium, copper, steel, or iron plating are the most largely used for the repair of parts. The essence of electoplating comes to the following. The part 1 (Fig. 14) is placed as a cathode into the electrolyte 2 containing metal salts used for coating the part. When direct current is passed from the source 3through the anode 4, the metal from the electrolyte is deposited on the surface of the part to be restored. Chromium plating is used for the restoration of spinning spindles, fluted and pressure rollers, shafts, axles, spindles and other parts with a wear not in excess of 0.1-0.2 m m per side. The part prepared for chromium plating must satisfy the following requirements: it must have a regular geometric shape and a high finish (8-9 class), it must be free from notches and scores, and be clean. The places on the parts which are not to be chromium plated must be insulated. An important drawback of a smooth chromium-plated coating is its low wettability with oil. For increasing the wettability porous chromium plating is used which is effected by mechanical, chemical, or electrochemical methods. Prior to chromium plating by the mechanical method recesses are made on the surface of the part to be restored in the shape of pores or grooves by knurling (on steel parts), or by sandblasting (on cast iron parts). Next, the cavities are coated by chromium plating.

text: The chemical method of chromium plating consists in shorttime etching of the chromium coating in diluted hydrochloric acid (1:1). In this way, the microcracks in the chromium coating arewidened and deepened. With the electrochemical method, the chromium coating is subjected to anode pickling by reversing the polarity (the chromium plated part becomes an anode). In microcracks the chromium is dissolved, and as a result the cracks become wider and deeper.

text: The quality of riveting is determined by exterior examination, knocking and random inspection of the head size using gauges and feelers; moreover the setting of the rivet rod is also checked (filling up of the hole by the rivet body). Knocking of rivet heads with a diameter up to 19 mm is carried out with a hammer weighing 250 g, and of rivets with heads over 19 m m in diameter— with a hammer weighing 400 g. When knocking with a hammer causes the vibration or displacement of the rivet head, the rivet should be sheared and replaced with a new one. When the rivets have cracks in the head, or the head has irregular tolerances of shape, with dimensions exceeding the tolerances established by standards and norms, the rivets must be sheared and replaced with new ones. Notching of the metal by a hobby tool to a depth over 0.5 m m is not allowed.

text: Axles and shafts. Intended for supporting rotating parts— pulleys, blocks, gears, sprockets, rollers, etc. Though slightly differing in design, axles and shafts operate in a different manner; axles support rotating parts, and therefore they are subject to the bending load from the mass of these parts and from the loads applied to them, while shafts are members of a mechanism transmitting the torque. Depending on operational conditions, the axles may be stationary or rotating together with the parts fitted on them (car wheels, blocks), while shafts are only rotatable.

text: Loads taken up by shafts and axles are transmitted to the bodies or frameworks of machines through supports, i.e. bearings. Depending on the kind of friction all the bearings are classified in sliding and rolling friction plain and antifriction bearings. The parts of axles and shafts which arein direct contact with the bearings have a common name— journals (Fig. 16). The journal transmitting to the bearing the radial load and disposed at the end of the shaft is called a pin (7) and that disposed in the middle of the shaft is called the neck (2). That part of the shaft which transmits the axial load to the bearings (5) is called the thrust journal (5) while the sliding bearing taking up this axial load is called the thrust bearing (4).

text: Axles are always straight while shafts may be straight, cranked, and flexible. Mostly, straight shafts are used. As classified by their design the shafts and axles m a y be smooth, stepped, solid, and hollow. For mounting gears, pulleys, couplings and bearings on the shafts and axles, adequate cylindrical or bevel mountings are provided with certain diameters and lengths. To fix these parts in axial direction the shafts are equipped with shoulders and 46 Chapter Three threading for fixing the parts with a nut, etc. For transmitting the torque to the shafts keyed, splined and pinned joints are used. Mostly solid shafts and axles are used, but in the case when the mass of parts must be reduced or it isnecessary to pass the shaft through another part, as for instance a tie rod, the shafts and axles are made hollow.

text: Axle and shaft bearings. Bearings may be classified according to the following features. For instance, depending on the kind of friction they may be classified into sliding or plain bearings in which the supporting part of the axle or shaft (journal, pin, neck, heel) slides on the interior surface of the bearing and into rolling or antifriction bearings in which the sliding friction is replaced by the rolling friction (this being achieved by the introduction of rollers or balls between the journal and the bushing). Depending on the direction of the load applied the bearings are subdivided into radial bearings taking up radial loads, thrust bearings taking up axial loads, and radial thrust bearings taking up radial and axial loads.

text: Sliding orplain bearings. The advantages presented by these bearings are: smaller dimensions as compared with the rolling antifriction bearings; the use of split bearings which may be mounted on the main journal of crankshafts; the operation with shafts rotating at a speed of 10 000 min-1 and higher; possible operation in water and other aggressive mediums under vibration and impact loads; the possibility of using large-size journals. The drawbacks of sliding bearings are the need of constant observation and continuous oiling, the reduced efficiency, the nonuniform wear of bearings and journals, the use of costly nonferrous metals and alloys (bronze, babbitt), and relatively long journals and linings.

All the lubricants are subdivided into liquid oils, consistent, and solid grease.

text: Liquid oils are the most largely used lubricants. As a rule, for oiling the machines petroleum oils find application. The most important characteristic of the oils is their viscosity. The viscosity or internal friction is the resistance against the shifting of one lubricant layer relative to the other. Viscosity m a y be dynamic or absolute and kinematic. Dynamic viscosity is determined by the hydrodynamic calculations of a given lubricant. Kinematic viscosity is determined by the time necessary for the flow of a preset amount of oil through a capillary tube under the action of gravity. The unit of kinematic viscosity is stokes (the name of the English scientist Stokes). text: Greases are obtained by adding thickening agents such as calcium and sodium oils into liquid oil. The most largely used greases on a calcium base are the cup greases and on a sodium base— constalines. Greases are employed with high loads and small rotational speeds of shafts and axles. Greases are entirely leakless (it is enough to use simple packings), completely fill the clearances between the rotating and stationary parts, may operate during a long period of time {ayear and more without change) and reliably protect the parts against corrosion. Greases present the following disadvantages: they are sensitive to changes in temperature, present a high internal friction and are difficult to replace. Usually greases are packed at the assembly of a unit and are periodically replenished by means of special cup oilers or a grease gun through grease cups.

text: Rigidcouplings are used in cases when a built-up shaft must operate as a whole one. Such couplings require a precise coincidence of connected shafts as the non-axiality appearing in the course of operation may cause bending and damaging of bearings. The simplest rigid coupling is a sleeve mounted with an interference fit on the ends of the shafts. The torque is transmitted by means of semi-circular or sunk keys. This kind of coupling is called an end sleeve. Wide application find flange couplings consisting of two flanged halfcouplings keyed on the ends of the shafts.

text: Jaw clutches consist of two half-couplings, the left half-coupling being attached on the shaft by means of a sunk key with an interference fit, while the right-hand one is fitted on the driven shaft by virtue of a sunk key and with a slide fit so that it may be displaced along the shaft axis by a forked shifter. On the faces of both halfcouplings there are provided protrusions (cams) and recesses. The cam profile may be rectangular or trapezoidal (which facilitates coupling engagement and allows the reverse motion without jolts). The use of jaw clutches is recommended when the shafts to be connected rotate at relatively slow speeds.

Both the friction and jaw clutches are used to prevent shaft misalignment. Special clutches are designed to protect the drive from overloads (breakages) and to transmit the torque only in one direction or at the preset rotational speed. text: Belt drives are a veriety of friction transmissions by a flexible connection, i.e. belting. Depending on the shape of the belt cross section the drives may be of the flat-belt, V-belt, and round-belt type. The advantages presented by the belt drive are the possibility of power transmission over long distances (up to 15 m and more), smooth and noiseless operation, the absence of sharp deviations in loads owing to flexible stretching of the belt, protection of mechanisms from overloads owing to the possible belt slippage, simplicity of design and the ease of operation, and the possibility of different arrangement of shafts in space. The drawbacks of belt drives are their large sizes, the inconstancy of the gear ratio due to belt slippage, the high load on the shafts and bearings which is necessary to ensure the preliminary tension of the belt and the short life of belts (1000-5000 h).

Depending on operation conditions, driving belts may be made of different materials, such as leather, rubberized cotton, and wool. Endless standard belts are used for high-speed drives which considerably enhances the quality of transmission, but their application is limited due to the complexity of their manufacturing. V-belts have a trapezoidal shape in cross section and are made of rubberized textile cord. The belt pulley consists of the rim carrying the belt, the hub keyed on the shaft, and the spokes or the disk connecting the rim with the hub. The shape of the rim working surface is determined by the kind of belt to be used.

text: Depending on their use, the gears are manufactured by different methods. For instance, for low-speed drives gears with cast teeth are employed. The precision of their manufacture is not high, but owing to the hard crust on the tooth surface its wear resistance is high. To improve the precision of gearing, the gears with cast teeth are sometimes subjected to additional mechanical treatment. At present, in mass production hot gear generation is used without further machining. As a rule the manufacture of gears consists of the following operations: the production of a blank (by casting, forging, or stamping) with further turning on a lathe; gear teeth cutting on milling machines, gear shapers, or other special machine tools; heat treatment (if such is needed); teeth finishing (by grinding, shaving, or lapping) for gears of not under the 7th class of precision.

text: Jamming (Fig. 20d)is observed in high-speed and heavily loaded transmissions. At the point of contact under the action of high pressure and temperature, oil is squeezed out and metal particles as if become welded and torn off from one of the surfaces. The build-up* is formed which scratches the working surfaces. A special oil is used to reduce jamming. Plastic shearing of the teeth surface layer is characteristic for heavily loaded slow speed transmissions with gearings made of materials of low hardness. To avoid this, it is necessary to increase tho hardness of the teeth material. In such gearings it is observed that the surface layer obtained by nitriding, cyaniding, and cementation, would peel off as a result of high contact stresses. Peeling is very dangerous as bits of metal getting between the teeth rapidly bring the whole gear transmission out of order.

text: Considering the hard working conditions the materials for the -worm gear must have good antifriction properties, high wear resistance and a low jamming ability. In modern transmissions the worms are made of carbon and alloy steel. In heavily loaded transmissions the worm is subjected to heat treatment (cementation, hardening, etc.) with subsequent grinding or polishing. The worm gears are mainly made of bronze, and for minor slow-speed gearing •cast iron is employed. Tin bronze is considered as the best material for worm gears. They are used for manufacturing heavily loaded gearings operating at high sliding speeds (up to 25 m/s). Tinless bronze is used for gearings operating at sliding speeds up to 10 m/s and cast iron for speeds up to 2 m/s.

text: Chain drives are largely used in textile machinery mainly as a stepdown transmission. Their main advantages are: the possibility of using smaller overall dimensions than in belt drives at considerable interaxial distances (up to 8 m), constant gear ratio (imas = = 8), high efficiency (up to 0.98), unlike in belt drives, lower loads on the shafts, and the possibility of imparting rotation to several shafts by one chain. The drawbacks presented by the chain drives are chain stretching due to wear in articulations, the high cost of the chain, the impossibility of reversing without stopping the machine, loud noise during operation and the necessity of a careful maintenance (adjustment, lubrication, and elimination of misalign­ ment).
